thread.title: State said it will seek town input on Great Creek solution
thread.title_full: State said it will seek town input on Great Creek solution

author: ohtadmin
title: State said it will seek town input on Great Creek solution
text:
State transportation officials said they are “open-minded” about solutions for the Great Creek span on North Road and will not proceed without speaking with the community.
Town Administrator Ed Mello, who met in September with the Rhode Island Department of Transportation and its director, Peter Alviti, briefed the town council at its Oct. 6 meeting. Referencing a presentation in May by Alviti’s team, he said there could be a perception among residents that the state supports building a 1,500-foot-long bridge over the creek.
“They left the impression that, perhaps mistakenly so, that was the option they selected,” he said. “That is not the case. We don’t want the community to be left with the impression that they have made a decision. … They are committed to hearing from the community before they move forward. They were very clear that they want community input.”
The state has presented five options for the section of road, which has been prone to flooding during storms and extremely high tides.
The first option was the $100 million bridge to replace the 90-year-old culvert. Skye Levin, an engineer with PHB, said having the bridge 10 feet above sea level is the “bomb-proof” option when considering 3 feet of sea-level rise by 2050 is “imminent.”
The second option, which is the cheapest, would entail abandoning the road. This choice, however, would eliminate an evacuation route while increasing traffic on East Shore Road.
The other options include keeping the status quo and expanding the hydraulic openings, which could be done with or without elevating the road. The conservation commission in July advised the councilors to reject the first option because the “Great Creek’s habitat and its flora and fauna would be better served with a design that is significantly smaller in scope and seeks to minimize environmental impact.” Mello said Alviti has taken that concern into account.
“The impact of that change of character is something that they are strongly considering,” he said.
Mello said the project is between 8-10 years away and “funding is still a challenge. It’s not a funded project as of this moment.”
Council President Nancy Beye said Alviti’s agency told her during a public meeting that Jamestown will have the final say about which option is chosen.
“We’re going to hold them to that,” she said.
Vice President Erik Brine asked if there was a deadline for the council to make its recommendation. Mello replied, “I don’t believe there’s a deadline.” He expects the conversation to continue within the next four to eight months.
“We can get a lot of opinions from everyone, and we should do that,” Brine said. “But, eventually we need to make a decision as a community and be able to project that decision in a timely manner so that we can bring together resources from a variety of places to get what we want.”
Mello said other municipally elected governing boards in Rhode Island have taken formal positions when DOT gets ready to improve its infrastructure in their cities and towns. The councilors could, for example, send a letter to Alviti saying they oppose the 100-foot-long span.
“I don’t know if they are held to that position,” Mello said, “but I’m certain that they will weigh that decision very heavily in the process. It was very clear to me that they are very open-minded about this project and want something the community embraces.”
Mello said the two sides also are working to coordinate projects. A water main on North Road from Narragansett Avenue to the treatment plant needs to be replaced. Doing that local job as the state fixes the bridge would make that project easier, he said.
